extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent examiners, policymakers, and stakeholders evaluating U.S. patent reform legislation
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the legal standards, definitional rules, and procedural requirements in a proposed U.S. patent reform bill (first-to-file, prior art, damages, post‑grant review, false marking, practitioner sanctions, etc.). Useful for practitioners and policymakers interpreting how the bill would change patent validity, remedies, and Office procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-availability standard for prior art (section 102(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: New section 102(a)(1) imposes a public-availability standard on the definition of all prior art enumerated by the bill; the clause 'or otherwise available to the public' applies to both 'public use' and 'on sale.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether an invention has been made available to the public is the same inquiry used to determine whether a document has become publicly accessible, generalized to account for non-document disclosures. This replaces earlier forfeiture doctrines and focuses prior art solely on disclosures that make the invention accessible to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'publicly accessible' document
rubrics_metrics.description: A document is publicly accessible if it has been disseminated or otherwise made available to the extent that persons interested and ordinarily skilled in the subject matter or art, exercising reasonable diligence, can locate it and recognize and comprehend therefrom the essentials of the claimed invention without need of further research or experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted from Cordis Corp. v. Boston Scientific Corp.; accessibility means interested members of the relevant public could obtain the information if they wanted to. Applied generally to non-document disclosures as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of modifier to series of antecedents
rubrics_metrics.description: Because 'or otherwise available to the public' is set off by a comma from preceding clauses, it should be read to apply to each of those antecedents (e.g., both 'public use' and 'on sale').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Finisar Corp. v. DirecTV Group on reading modifiers in series; supports interpreting the statutory phrase as a public‑availability test across listed prior-art categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of inherency as basis for anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the doctrine of inherency, if an element is not expressly disclosed in a prior art reference, the reference will still be deemed to anticipate a subsequent claim if the missing element is necessarily present in the thing described in the reference and it would be so recognized by persons of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to both published references and products sold to the public; once a product is sold, any invention inherent to that product becomes publicly available prior art (Rosco, Inc. v. Mirror Lite Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolition of traditional forfeiture doctrines (on-sale/public-use) in favor of public-availability
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill eliminates patent forfeiture doctrines that caused penal consequences for non‑public uses or secret sales and replaces them with a general public-availability test for prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: prevent extreme results (e.g., private demonstrations or single-use gifts deemed 'public use'), reduce discovery burdens, and limit prior art to disclosures that made the invention available to the public rather than to multiple policy goals (prompt filing, limiting commercialization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art geographic scope expanded (foreign sales/uses count)
rubrics_metrics.description: The elimination of geographic restrictions on the definition of prior art means sales and uses occurring overseas will also constitute prior art if they made the invention available to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because overseas secret sales/uses could be fraudulently asserted, the public-availability standard is necessary to ensure independent validation and to reduce risk of fraudulent invalidation based on unverifiable foreign secret uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-grant review scope and timing (first nine months)
rubrics_metrics.description: Creates a new post-grant review in which a patent can be challenged on any validity ground during the first nine months after its issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challengers will be estopped in litigation from raising only those issues that were raised and decided in the post-grant review (as opposed to broader estoppel applied in inter partes reexamination). Procedural design intended to make post-grant review administrable and limit harassment/delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter partes review estoppel limited by 'reasonably' could have been raised
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill softens the could-have-raised estoppel applied by inter partes review against subsequent civil litigation by adding the modifier 'reasonably.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estoppel applies to issues that were 'reasonably' raised and decided in the administrative proceeding, narrowing the scope of barred issues in subsequent litigation compared to 'could-have-raised' formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter partes reexamination procedural changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Eliminates the current requirement that an inter partes reexamination be terminated if litigation results in a final judgment and removes the bar on challenging pre-1999 patents in inter partes proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All patents can now be challenged in inter partes review; termination rules changed to allow proceedings to continue after litigation concludes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel in post-grant review limited to issues raised and decided
rubrics_metrics.description: Challengers who use post-grant review are estopped in litigation from raising only those issues that were raised and decided in the post-grant review (not all issues that could have been raised).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is narrower than prior estoppel standards and is intended to balance administrative review with litigation rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 115: Director may require earlier inventor oaths/declarations when claiming benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: New section 115(g) allows the Director to require an applicant claiming the benefit of an earlier-filed application to include copies of previous inventor's oaths used in those applications; the Office cannot begin examining an application until it knows who those inventors are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: inventor identity determines which prior art is counted; later-filed applications are not currently required to name inventors by statute, so requiring past oaths helps determine entitlement to benefit/priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee right to seek broadening reissue within two years
rubrics_metrics.description: Modifies section 251 to allow an assignee who applied for a patent to also seek broadening reissue of the patent within two years of its issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent with expanded assignee rights elsewhere in the bill; Office has historically allowed unopposed assignee reissues when inventor does not oppose—this makes that permissible by statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of qui tam false-marking suits; government and competitor remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (1) of section 2(k) eliminates the qui tam remedy for false marking, allows the United States to continue to seek the $500-per-article fine, and allows competitors who suffered competitive injury to seek compensatory damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aimed at reducing opportunistic high-volume false-marking litigation by private relators; United States can pursue public harm, competitors can sue for actual injury; changes made fully retroactive by paragraph (2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale on false marking: marking's primary purpose is to inform competitors
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent marking's primary purpose is to inform competitors (not consumers) that a product is patented; false-marking suits often arose over expired but physically marked products or disputes over coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of marking lag and cost to retool molds, retroactive qui tam recovery was disproportionate to actual harm; revised section 292(b) aims to restore equilibrium by focusing on competitive injury and government enforcement for public harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 2(l): statute of limitations for section 32 proceedings (exclude from practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: A section 32 proceeding to exclude an attorney from practice before the Office must be initiated either within 10 years of when the underlying misconduct occurred, or within 1 year of when the misconduct is reported to the PTO office charged with conducting section 32 proceedings, whichever is earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 10-year outward limit chosen to allow proceedings for the vast bulk of misconduct while keeping within time when recollections are reliable. Paragraph (2) requires the Office to report biennially to Congress on incidents that would have been investigated but for the 10-year limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 2(m): SBA report on first-to-file impact on small businesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Requires the Small Business Administration to report to Congress on the expected impact of the first-to-file system on small businesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges competing views: first-to-file may burden small entities by requiring earlier filings/more applications for complex inventions, but provisional applications and harmonization with global first-to-file systems could produce benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition rule to first-to-file (18-month effective date and application-level transition)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application contains or contained a claim to an invention with an effective filing date that is 18 months after the date of enactment, the entire application is subject to the first-to-file regime; reissues and continuations of first-to-invent patents remain subject to first-to-invent rules if they introduce no new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows applicants to flip forward into first-to-file but prevents flipping back; provides remedies where interfering patents straddle first-to-invent and first-to-file regimes by subjecting later-conceived patents to first-to-invent where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior-user rights study (Director report)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 2(n) requires the Director to report on the desirability of authorizing prior-user rights, particularly given adoption of first-to-file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directed report to assess balancing between first-to-file benefits and protection for prior users of technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on use of comparable-license evidence for damages valuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Court decisions (Lucent, ResQNet.com, Wordtech) restrict use of licenses for other patents to value the patent in suit: kinship alone is insufficient; comparable licenses must show significance to licensed products and have an economic or other link to the technology in question; comparisons must account for technological and economic differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These judicial limits reduce reliance on supposedly comparable licenses as manipulable and subjective metrics; they require demonstrable connection between the comparable license and the product/technology being valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule-of-thumb (25 percent rule) inadmissibility for baseline royalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniloc holds that the 25 percent rule of thumb is a fundamentally flawed tool for determining a baseline royalty rate and is inadmissible under Daubert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimony based on the 25% rule is to be excluded as unreliable; parties must rely on sound economic linkage and admissible methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on entire market value damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Lucent restricts awarding damages based on the entire market value of the infringing product unless there is substantial evidence that the patented invention was the basis for consumer demand for the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties must show that the patented feature drove consumer demand; otherwise damages should be apportioned and cannot be based on whole-product value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of treble damages role (deterrence of willful infringement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The present bill makes no changes to the standard for awards of treble damages; treble damages play an important deterrent role to discourage deliberate copying and make licensing the economically preferable option.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee views proposed 2009 bill restrictions on treble damages as overbroad; preserving enhancement authority aims to deter manufacturers from choosing to infringe when commercially tempted to copy a patented feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 298: bar on adverse inference from failure to obtain opinion of counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: Adds section 298 to bar courts and juries from drawing an adverse inference from an accused infringer’s failure to obtain an opinion of counsel on infringement or from failure to waive privilege and disclose such an opinion; applies to willfulness and inducement findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects attorney-client privilege and reduces incentive to obtain litigation-tailored opinions; legislatively abrogates Broadcom Corp. v. Qualcomm (which had held such failure could be probative of intent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative-procedure design goal: prevent abuse/harassment in post‑grant proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes to inter partes and post-grant review aim to make these systems administrable by the PTO and impose procedural limits to prevent abuse of proceedings for harassment or delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes timing, estoppel, institution/discretion changes (e.g., PTO allowed to stay derivation proceedings, institute on substantial evidence of derivation, allow civil action under revised section 291 in lieu of section 135).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation remedy procedural changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Modifies remedies for derivation: new simplified section 135 proceeding with Office authority to implement via regulations; Office may stay derivation pending ex parte reexamination, IPR, or PGR of the earlier‑filed patent and may decline to institute absent substantial evidence of derivation; parties may instead challenge via civil action under revised section 291.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural streamlining at PTO’s suggestion, giving PTO flexibility and limiting unnecessary institution of administrative derivation proceedings.
